notes.meaning: God calls every nation and people across the earth to come close and hear his royal summons. He addresses the entire world and everything in it because his coming judgment concerns all humanity, not just Israel. When the Lord speaks to the nations, everyone is required to pay attention.

The Lord is deeply angry with all the nations and their armies that rebel against him. He devotes them to destruction, which means he has marked them out for total ruin. Once God determines their sentence, their downfall is completely certain.

The fallen soldiers will be left unburied in the open fields, which was considered an awful disgrace in the ancient world. So many will be killed that the air will fill with a terrible smell and the mountains will seem to melt with streams of blood. This vivid language shows how crushing the defeat will be.

Isaiah pictures the sky dissolving and rolling up like a parchment scroll, while the stars drop like withered leaves from a grapevine or a fig tree. These dramatic pictures show that when the Lord steps in to judge the world, the entire universe feels the shock. Earthly rulers will fall just as easily as dying leaves.

differ.view: Terrified people experience God's earthly judgments so intensely that it seems to them as though the heavens and the earth are falling apart.
This describes the literal end of the world, when the physical heavens and stars will actually be dissolved on the final day of judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the phrase describing the host of heaven might be a later addition to the original Hebrew text.

notes.meaning: God speaks of his sword being prepared and sharpened in heaven before it comes down in judgment upon Edom. The Edomites were old enemies of God's people, descended from Jacob's brother Esau, and here they represent all corrupt nations. The people marked for destruction cannot escape God's decree.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Edom is understood here not just as a single ancient nation, but as a poetic symbol standing for every hostile power that opposes God.

notes.meaning: The coming judgment is pictured as a massive animal sacrifice taking place in Bozrah, a major fortified city of Edom. The blood of lambs, goats, and rams stands for people of every rank and station who face God's justice. Because they rejected the true God, they become the victims in his great reckoning.

Fierce wild oxen and young bulls will fall in the slaughter alongside the smaller animals. These powerful beasts represent Edom's proud princes and military commanders who thought they were invincible. Their land will be thoroughly soaked with blood, showing that no earthly power can resist God.

The Lord has appointed a specific day and year to settle his dispute with those who mistreated his people. He brings retribution, which means fair payback, to defend Zion against all who attacked her. God will not let the cruelty of Edom and other enemies go unanswered forever.

Edom's rivers and soil are pictured turning into thick tar and burning sulfur. This description reminds readers of the ancient destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, which lay near Edom's borders. The fertile ground will be transformed into an uninhabitable, fiery wasteland.

The fire will not be put out, and its smoke will rise continuously to show permanent destruction. Because Edom once refused to let the Israelites travel peacefully through their territory, now no traveler will ever pass through Edom again. The ruined land stands as a lasting warning across all generations.

Desert birds, owls, and ravens will move in and take over the land where humans once lived. The Lord stretches out a measuring line of chaos and emptiness over the cities, marking them out for demolition rather than building. The land is reduced back to the wild, empty state that existed before creation.

There will be no nobles left to choose a king, and all of Edom's rulers will vanish into nothing. The government and social order will collapse completely. Nobody will be willing or able to step up and lead the broken nation.

Thorny weeds, briers, and nettles will grow up through the broken stone of once-grand palaces and fortresses. Wild dogs, jackals, and ostriches will make their homes where royalty once lived. What was once magnificent human architecture will become an eerie haven for wild animals.

Wild cats, jackals, and desert beasts will meet among the ruins and call out to one another. Night creatures will settle there in safety because no human beings remain to disturb them. The once-thriving nation is now a spooky and silent desert sanctuary for wild life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word translated night creature may reflect an ancient Near Eastern folklore term for a night-demon thought to haunt desolate ruins.

notes.meaning: Owls and birds of prey will build their nests, lay eggs, and hatch their young among the fallen stones. These creatures will gather with their mates without fear, showing that the ruins have become their lasting nursery. The complete absence of human life makes the area a safe haven for wild animals.

Readers are challenged to open the Lord's written word and check this prophecy against the facts when it happens. Not one of these wild creatures will be missing, and none will lack a mate, because God's mouth ordered it and his Spirit gathers them. God's promises in Scripture are completely dependable in every detail.

The Lord divides the ruined territory among the wild animals by lot, just as he once divided the Promised Land among the tribes of Israel. These beasts will own Edom as their permanent home, living there from generation to generation. God controls the boundaries of all nations and gives the land to whomever he pleases.
